claim: The moon jellyfish Aurelia coerulea (formerly A. aurita sp. 1 strain) has eight arms that facilitate morphological tracking in ephyrae.
source: We focused on the moon jellyfish Aurelia coerulea (formerly A. aurita sp. 1 strain), specifically on the ephyra, whose eight arms facilitate morphological tracking (Figure 1b).
evidence: This is stated directly in the text describing the experimental model organism.

claim: Aurelia ephyrae are about 3 mm in diameter.
source: About 3 mm in diameter, Aurelia ephyrae regenerate the tips of arms and the distal sensory organ rhopalium, but upon more dramatic amputations such as removing a whole arm or halving the body, rapidly reorganize existing body parts and regain radial symmetry (Figure 1c).
evidence: This is a direct measurement stated in the text.

claim: Aurelia ephyrae regenerate the tips of arms and the distal sensory organ rhopalium.
source: About 3 mm in diameter, Aurelia ephyrae regenerate the tips of arms and the distal sensory organ rhopalium, but upon more dramatic amputations such as removing a whole arm or halving the body, rapidly reorganize existing body parts and regain radial symmetry (Figure 1c).
evidence: This is an observation stated in the text about the regenerative capacity of ephyrae.

claim: Upon dramatic amputations such as removing a whole arm or halving the body, Aurelia ephyrae rapidly reorganize existing body parts and regain radial symmetry.
source: About 3 mm in diameter, Aurelia ephyrae regenerate the tips of arms and the distal sensory organ rhopalium, but upon more dramatic amputations such as removing a whole arm or halving the body, rapidly reorganize existing body parts and regain radial symmetry (Figure 1c).
evidence: This is an observation stated in the text about the response to injury.

claim: Symmetrization in Aurelia ephyrae occurs rapidly within 1–3 days and robustly across conditions.
source: Observed across four scyphozoan species, symmetrization occurs rapidly within 1–3 days and robustly across conditions (Abrams et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by data from a previous study cited in the text.

claim: Ephyrae that symmetrized matured into medusae.
source: Ephyrae that symmetrized matured into medusae, whereas ephyrae that failed to symmetrize and simply healed the wound grew abnormally.
evidence: This is an observation stated in the text about developmental outcomes.

claim: Ephyrae that failed to symmetrize and simply healed the wound grew abnormally.
source: Ephyrae that symmetrized matured into medusae, whereas ephyrae that failed to symmetrize and simply healed the wound grew abnormally.
evidence: This is an observation stated in the text about developmental outcomes.

claim: In the natural habitat experiment, 2 out of 18 ephyrae regenerated a small arm.
source: Two weeks after amputation, most ephyrae indeed symmetrized, but in 2 out of 18 animals a small arm grew (Figure 1c).
evidence: This is a direct quantitative observation from the experiment.

claim: Despite symmetrization being the more robust response to injury, an inherent ability to regenerate arm is present in Aurelia ephyrae and can be naturally manifest.
source: This observation suggests that, despite symmetrization being the more robust response to injury, an inherent ability to regenerate arm is present and can be naturally manifest.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observation of arm regeneration in the natural habitat.

claim: Arm regenerates in Aurelia show multiple tissues regrown in the right locations: circulatory canals, muscle, neurons, and rhopalium.
source: In the few conditions where regeneration occurred, arm regenerates show multiple tissues regrown in the right locations: circulatory canals, muscle, neurons, and rhopalium (Figure 2c–e).
evidence: This is supported by histological data shown in the figures.

claim: The arm regenerates in Aurelia contracted synchronously with the original arms, demonstrating a functional neuromuscular network.
source: The arm regenerates contracted synchronously with the original arms (Video 1), demonstrating a functional neuromuscular network.
evidence: This is supported by video evidence showing synchronized contraction.

claim: The extent of arm regeneration in Aurelia varied, from small to almost fully sized arms.
source: The extent of arm regeneration varied, from small to almost fully sized arms (Figure 2b).
evidence: This is an observation stated in the text and shown in the figure.

claim: Of the three arms removed in Aurelia, if regeneration occurred, generally one arm regenerated (67%), occasionally two arms (32%), and rarely three arms (1%).
source: Of the three arms removed, if regeneration occurred, generally one arm regenerated (67%), occasionally two arms (32%), and rarely three arms (1%, of the 4270 total ephyrae quantified in this study).
evidence: This is a quantitative summary of the regeneration data.

claim: The frequency of regeneration in Aurelia varied across clutches (strobilation cohorts).
source: Finally, the frequency of regeneration varied across clutches, that is, strobilation cohorts.
evidence: This is an observation stated in the text about experimental variability.

claim: The variability in regeneration frequency in Aurelia was not entirely due to genetic differences, as it manifested across clonal populations.
source: We verified that the variability was not entirely due to genetic differences, as it manifested across clonal populations (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by experiments with clonal populations shown in the supplementary figure.

claim: There appears to be stochasticity in the occurrence of arm regeneration in Aurelia and the extent to which regeneration proceeds.
source: Thus, there appears to be stochasticity in the occurrence of arm regeneration in Aurelia and the extent to which regeneration proceeds.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observed variability in regeneration.

claim: Modulation of developmental pathways often implicated in regeneration literature (e.g., Wnt, Bmp, and Tgfß) did not produce effect in the Aurelia screen.
source: Notably, modulation of developmental pathways often implicated in regeneration literature (e.g., Wnt, Bmp, and Tgfß) did not produce effect in the screen (Figure 2—source data 1)—although we do not rule out their involvement in other capacity, for example, in downstream patterning.
evidence: This is stated based on the screening results.

claim: Water current is a necessary condition for promoting regeneration in Aurelia.
source: We first identified a necessary condition: water current.
evidence: This is stated as a finding from the screen.

claim: The requirement for current for promoting regeneration in Aurelia is interesting because ephyrae can recover from injury by symmetrizing in stagnant water.
source: The requirement for current for promoting regeneration is interesting because ephyrae can recover from injury by symmetrizing in stagnant water (Figure 1c).
evidence: This is an observation comparing regeneration requirements to symmetrization requirements.

claim: A specific physiological state is required for enabling regenerative response in Aurelia.
source: Thus, a specific physiological state is required for enabling regenerative response.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the water current requirement.

claim: In the presence of current, increasing food amount increases the frequency of arm regeneration in Aurelia.
source: In this permissive condition, the first factor that promotes regeneration is the nutrient level: increasing food amount increases the frequency of arm regeneration.
evidence: This is stated as a finding from the experiments.

claim: Higher food amounts reproducibly increased regeneration frequency in Aurelia (95% CI [4.7, 12.1-fold], p<10–4).
source: With these measurement and statistical methodologies, we found that although the baseline regeneration frequency varied across clutches, higher food amounts reproducibly increased regeneration frequency (Figure 3c). The magnitude of the increase varied (Figure 3g, 95% confidence interval [CI] [4.7, 12.1-fold]), but the increase was reproducible (95% CI excludes 1) and statistically significant (p<10–4).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data.

claim: Administering 500 nM insulin led to a reproducible (95% CI [1.1, 5.0-fold], p<0.05) and statistically significant increase in regeneration frequency in Aurelia.
source: Administering insulin led to a reproducible (Figure 3g, 95% CI [1.1, 5.0-fold]) and statistically significant (p<0.05) increase in regeneration frequency.
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data.

claim: The insulin receptor is conserved in Aurelia.
source: We verified that the insulin receptor is conserved in Aurelia (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by phylogenetic analysis shown in the supplementary figure.

claim: The insulin effect in Aurelia was unlikely to be due to non-specific addition of proteins, since bovine serum albumin (BSA) at the same molarity showed no statistically significant effect.
source: The insulin effect was unlikely to be due to non-specific addition of proteins, since bovine serum albumin (BSA) at the same molarity showed no statistically significant effect (Figure 3—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is a control experiment to verify specificity of the insulin effect.

claim: Hypoxia led to a reproducible (95% CI [1.4, 12.0-fold], p<0.01) and statistically significant increase in regeneration frequency in Aurelia.
source: Hypoxia led to a reproducible (Figure 3g, 95% CI [1.4, 12.0-fold]) and statistically significant (p<0.01) increase in regeneration frequency.
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data.

claim: The ancient oxygen sensor HIFα is present in Aurelia.
source: We verified that the ancient oxygen sensor HIFα is present in Aurelia (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by phylogenetic analysis shown in the supplementary figure.

claim: The hypoxia effect on regeneration in Aurelia was due to reduced oxygen rather than increased nitrogen, since reducing oxygen using argon flow similarly increased regeneration frequency.
source: We verified that the effect was due to reduced oxygen rather than increased nitrogen, since reducing oxygen using argon flow similarly increased regeneration frequency (Figure 3—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is a control experiment to verify the mechanism of the hypoxia effect.

claim: Nutrient level, insulin, and hypoxia can act synergistically to promote regeneration in Aurelia, but the effect appears to eventually saturate.
source: The factors can act synergistically (e.g., insulin and high nutrient level), but the effect appears to eventually saturate (e.g., hypoxia and high nutrient level).
evidence: This is an observation about the interaction of different treatments.

claim: Nutrient level in Aurelia improved all phenotypic metrics: not only more ephyrae regenerated in higher nutrients, more ephyrae regenerated multiple arms, longer arms, and arms with rhopalia.
source: Nutrient level strikingly improved all phenotypic metrics: not only more ephyrae regenerated in higher nutrients, more ephyrae regenerated multiple arms, longer arms, and arms with rhopalia.
evidence: This is a summary of the phenotypic analysis presented in the supplementary figures.

claim: While insulin induced more Aurelia ephyrae to regenerate multiple arms, hypoxia induced largely single-arm regenerates.
source: Most strikingly, while insulin induced more ephyrae to regenerate multiple arms, hypoxia induced largely single-arm regenerates, for example, hypoxia experiments 3 and 5 in Figure 3—figure supplement 5c.
evidence: This is an observation about differential effects of treatments on regeneration phenotypes.

claim: While all factors increased the probability to regenerate in Aurelia, they had differential effects on the regeneration phenotypes, suggesting a decoupling to a certain extent between the regulation of the decision to regenerate and the regulation of the subsequent morphogenesis.
source: Thus, while all factors increased the probability to regenerate, they had differential effects on the regeneration phenotypes, suggesting a decoupling to a certain extent between the regulation of the decision to regenerate and the regulation of the subsequent morphogenesis.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the differential phenotypic effects of treatments.

claim: All three factors (nutrients, insulin, hypoxia) induced growth in Aurelia: treated ephyrae are larger than control ephyrae.
source: Notably, all three factors induced growth: treated ephyrae are larger than control ephyrae (Figure 3—figure supplement 7).
evidence: This is supported by measurements shown in the supplementary figure.

claim: Branched amino acids supplementation correlates positively with protein synthesis and growth, and in particular, L-leucine appears to recapitulate most of the anabolic effects of high amino acid diet.
source: The growth effect is interesting because of essential amino acids that must be obtained from food, branched amino acids supplementation correlates positively with protein synthesis and growth, and in particular, L-leucine appears to recapitulate most of the anabolic effects of high amino acid diet (Lynch and Adams, 2014; Stipanuk, 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Animals typically have a poor ability to metabolize leucine, such that the extracellular concentrations of leucine fluctuate with dietary consumption.
source: Animals typically have a poor ability to metabolize leucine, such that the extracellular concentrations of leucine fluctuate with dietary consumption (Wolfson et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Dietary leucine directly influences cellular metabolism.
source: As a consequence, dietary leucine directly influences cellular metabolism.
evidence: This is an inference based on the poor ability to metabolize leucine.

claim: Feeding amputated Aurelia ephyrae with leucine led to increased growth.
source: Feeding amputated ephyrae with leucine indeed led to increased growth (Figure 3—figure supplement 6).
evidence: This is supported by measurements shown in the supplementary figure.

claim: Leucine treatment led to a significant increase in regeneration frequency in Aurelia (95% CI [2.5, 6.6-fold], p<10–4).
source: Assessing arm regeneration in the leucine-supplemented ephyrae, we observed a significant increase in the regeneration frequency (Figure 3f–g, 95% CI [2.5, 6.6-fold], p<10–4).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data.

claim: Leucine treatment phenocopies the effect of high nutrients in Aurelia, improving all measured phenotypic metrics: increasing multi-arm regeneration, the length of arm regenerate, and the frequency of rhopalia formation.
source: Furthermore, leucine treatment phenocopies the effect of high nutrients, improving all measured phenotypic metrics: increasing multi-arm regeneration, the length of arm regenerate, and the frequency of rhopalia formation (Figure 3—figure supplements 5 and 6).
evidence: This is supported by phenotypic analysis shown in the supplementary figures.

claim: Abundant nutrients, the growth factor insulin, reduced oxygen level, and the amino acid L-leucine promote appendage regeneration in Aurelia ephyra.
source: These experiments demonstrate that abundant nutrients, the growth factor insulin, reduced oxygen level, and the amino acid L-leucine promote appendage regeneration in Aurelia ephyra.
evidence: This is a summary of the experimental findings.

claim: The identified factors (nutrients, insulin, reduced oxygen, L-leucine) are fundamental physiological factors across animals.
source: The identified factors are fundamental physiological factors across animals.
evidence: This is a statement about the generality of the factors.

claim: Drosophila, along with beetles and butterflies, belong to the holometabolans—a vast group of insects that undergo complete metamorphosis, and that as whole, do not regenerate limbs or other appendages as adults.
source: Drosophila, along with beetles and butterflies, belong to the holometabolans—a vast group of insects that undergo complete metamorphosis, and that as whole, do not regenerate limbs or other appendages as adults (Das, 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Larval stages of Drosophila have imaginal disks, undifferentiated precursors of adult appendages such as the legs and antennae, and portions of imaginal disks have been shown to regenerate.
source: Larval stages have imaginal disks, undifferentiated precursors of adult appendages such as the legs and antennae, and portions of imaginal disks have been shown to regenerate (Worley et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: No regrown tibia was found in the 860 control Drosophila flies examined.
source: No regrown tibia was found in the 860 control flies examined (Figure 4b–c).
evidence: This is a direct quantitative observation from the experiment.

claim: In treated Drosophila flies, at 7–21 days post-amputation, a few regrown tibias were observed (1.0%, N=387).
source: But remarkably, at 7–21 days post-amputation (dpa), a few regrown tibias were observed (1.0%, N=387; Figure 4d–e).
evidence: This is a direct quantitative observation from the experiment.

claim: The regrown tibias in Drosophila culminate in reformed joints, articulating from which appears to be the beginning of a next segment.
source: The regrown tibias culminate in reformed joints, articulating from which appears to be the beginning of a next. segment.
evidence: This is an observation stated in the text about the morphology of regrown tibias.

claim: Control Drosophila tibia stumps showed melanized clots at the tips within 1–3 dpa, as expected from normal wound healing process.
source: Control tibia stumps showed melanized clots at the tips within 1–3 dpa (Figure 4b), as expected from normal wound healing process (Rämet et al., 2002), while some treated tibias showed no clot (12.1%, N=387) and the tips stained positively with DAPI instead (14 out of 16 tibias examined; Figure 4f).
evidence: This is an observation supported by a citation to previous literature on wound healing.

claim: Some treated Drosophila tibias showed no clot (12.1%, N=387) and the tips stained positively with DAPI instead (14 out of 16 tibias examined).
source: Control tibia stumps showed melanized clots at the tips within 1–3 dpa (Figure 4b), as expected from normal wound healing process (Rämet et al., 2002), while some treated tibias showed no clot (12.1%, N=387) and the tips stained positively with DAPI instead (14 out of 16 tibias examined; Figure 4f).
evidence: This is a direct quantitative observation from the experiment.

claim: Induction of regenerative response in Drosophila was observed across genetic backgrounds, in Oregon R and Canton S wild-type strains.
source: Induction of regenerative response was observed across genetic backgrounds, in Oregon R, as discussed, and Canton S wild-type strains (Figure 4—figure supplement 1a).
evidence: This is stated as an observation from experiments in different strains.

claim: Control Drosophila tibia stumps showed near-zero percent change in length (mean –0.3%, 95% CI [–3.8, 3.2%], N=116).
source: Control tibia stumps showed near-zero percent change in length (Figure 5d; mean –0.3%, 95% CI [–3.8, 3.2%], N=116).
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from the single-fly tracking experiment.

claim: 49% of treated Drosophila flies showed growth beyond the 95% CIs of the control distribution (N=150).
source: By contrast, 49% of treated flies showed growth beyond the 95% CIs of the control distribution (Figure 5f; N=150).
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from the single-fly tracking experiment.

claim: The control and treated length change distributions in Drosophila are statistically different (p<0.0001***, nonparametric Kruskal-Wallis test).
source: We verified that the control and treated length change distributions are statistically different (p<0.0001***, nonparametric Kruskal-Wallis test).
evidence: This is a statistical analysis of the experimental data.

claim: No sex-based differences in regenerative response were observed in Drosophila.
source: No sex-based differences in response were observed (Figure 5—figure supplement 1a).
evidence: This is stated as an observation from the analysis.

claim: Five Drosophila flies showed reformed tibia segments: showing a tapering end (N=150), what appeared to be a joint, and the beginning of the next segment.
source: Finally, reproducing what was observed in the bulk experiments, five flies showed reformed tibia segments: showing a tapering end (N=150; Figure 5h), what appeared to be a joint (Figure 5i), and the beginning of the next segment (Figure 5j).
evidence: This is a direct quantitative observation from the experiment.

claim: A scanning electron micrograph of a regrown Drosophila hindlimb tibia morphologically confirms the regenerated joint as a tibial/tarsal joint.
source: A scanning electron micrograph of a regrown hindlimb tibia (the top tibia in Figure 4e, taken 1 week later) morphologically confirms the regenerated joint as a tibial/tarsal joint.
evidence: This is stated based on electron microscopy analysis.

claim: The regenerated Drosophila joint shows the expected bilateral symmetry of a tibial/tarsal joint with rounded projections at the posterior and anterior end called condyles.
source: The joint-like structure shows the expected bilateral symmetry of a tibial/tarsal joint (as opposed to, e.g., the radially symmetrical tarsal/tarsal joints; Mirth and Akam, 2002) with rounded projections at the posterior and anterior end (arrows in Figure 5k). These projections, called condyles, function as points of articulation between opposing leg segments.
evidence: This is an observation supported by a citation to previous literature on joint morphology.

claim: A unique feature of the tibial/tarsal joint of the Drosophila hindlimb (but not of fore or midlimb) is an additional ventral projection between the side condyles, which serves to restrain bending of the leg upward.
source: Finally, a unique feature of the tibial/tarsal joint of the hindlimb (but not of fore or midlimb) is an additional ventral projection between the side condyles (Mirth and Akam, 2002), which serves to restrain bending of the leg upward.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous literature on joint morphology.

claim: The ventral projection is present in the regenerated Drosophila joint.
source: The ventral projection is indeed present in the regenerated joint (arrow in Figure 5k).
evidence: This is an observation from the electron microscopy analysis.

claim: Patterned regenerative response can be induced from adult Drosophila limbs for the first time.
source: Altogether, these data demonstrate for the first time that patterned regenerative response can be induced from adult Drosophila limbs.
evidence: This is a summary statement of the novelty of the findings.

claim: One sign that limb regeneration may be feasible in humans is that fingertips regenerate.
source: One sign that limb regeneration may be feasible in humans is that fingertips regenerate (Illingworth, 1974).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: The mammalian model for studying limb regeneration is the house mouse, Mus musculus, which like humans, regenerates digit tips.
source: The mammalian model for studying limb regeneration is the house mouse, Mus musculus, which like humans, regenerates digit tips.
evidence: This is a statement about the model system used.

claim: Although proximal regions of mouse digits do not regenerate, increasing evidence suggests that they have inherent regenerative capacity.
source: Although proximal regions of digits do not regenerate, increasing evidence suggests that they have inherent regenerative capacity.
evidence: This is a statement about the current understanding of mouse digit regeneration.

claim: In adult mice, implanting developmental signals in amputated digits led to specific tissue induction, that is, bone growth with Bmp4 or joint-like structure with Bmp9.
source: In adult mice, implanting developmental signals in amputated digits led to specific tissue induction, that is, bone growth with Bmp4 or joint-like structure with Bmp9 (Yu et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: In neonatal mice, reactivation of the embryonic gene lin28 led to distal phalange regrowth.
source: In neonates, reactivation of the embryonic gene lin28 led to distal phalange regrowth (Shyh-Chang et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: While patterned phalange regeneration can be induced in newborn mice, induction in adults so far involves a fine-tuned stimulation.
source: Thus, while patterned phalange regeneration can be induced in newborns, induction in adults so far involves a fine-tuned stimulation, for example, to elongate bone and then make joint, Bmp4 was first administered followed by Bmp9 in a timed manner.
evidence: This is a summary of the current state of knowledge about mouse digit regeneration.

claim: Amputation that removes <30% of P3 length in mouse digits, that cuts within the nail, readily regenerates.
source: Amputation that removes <30% of P3 length, that cuts within the nail, readily regenerates, whereas amputation that removes >60% of P3 length, corresponding to removing almost the entire visible nail, does not regenerate (Figure 6c; Chamberlain et al., 2017; Lehoczky et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Amputation that removes >60% of P3 length in mouse digits, corresponding to removing almost the entire visible nail, does not regenerate.
source: Amputation that removes <30% of P3 length, that cuts within the nail, readily regenerates, whereas amputation that removes >60% of P3 length, corresponding to removing almost the entire visible nail, does not regenerate (Figure 6c; Chamberlain et al., 2017; Lehoczky et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: No regeneration was observed in the control mice (N=34 digits, 17 mice).
source: As expected for amputation proximal to the nail, no regeneration was observed in the control mice (N=34 digits, 17 mice).
evidence: This is a direct quantitative observation from the experiment.

claim: 18.8% of the treated mouse digits (N=48 digits, 24 mice) showed various extents of regenerative response.
source: By contrast, 18.8% of the treated digits (N=48 digits, 24 mice) showed various extents of regenerative response (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a direct quantitative observation from the experiment.

claim: The increase in regeneration frequency in mouse digits due to the treatment is statistically significant (95% CI [8, 30%], p=0.0019,**).
source: The increase in regeneration frequency due to the treatment is statistically significant (95% CI [8, 30%], p=0.0019,**, Student's t-test).
evidence: This is a statistical analysis of the experimental data.

claim: In one mouse digit, an almost complete regrowth of the distal phalange and the nail was observed.
source: In one digit, an almost complete regrowth of the distal phalange and the nail was observed (Figure 6g).
evidence: This is an observation from the experiment shown in the figure.

claim: In one mouse digit amputated at the proximal P3 transecting the os hole, by 7 weeks, the P3 bone was almost completely regrown.
source: Skeletal staining of the portion removed from this digit (Figure 6j) shows that it was amputated at the proximal P3 transecting the os hole. By 7 weeks, skeletal staining of the regrown digit (Figure 6j) shows that the P3 bone was almost completely regrown.
evidence: This is an observation from the experiment shown in the figure.

claim: The regrown P3 in mouse shows trabecular appearance that is similar in general structure but not identical to the original P3.
source: The regrown P3 shows trabecular appearance that is similar in general structure but not identical to the original P3.
evidence: This is an observation about the morphology of the regrown bone.

claim: In one mouse digit amputated across the P2 bone, removing the entire epiphyseal cap along with the sesamoid bone, the epiphyseal cap was regrown, along with its associated sesamoid bone.
source: Skeletal staining of the portion removed from this digit shows that it was amputated across the P2 bone, removing the entire epiphyseal cap along with the sesamoid bone (Figure 6k). Skeletal staining of the regenerating digit shows that the epiphyseal cap was regrown, along with its associated sesamoid bone.
evidence: This is an observation from the experiment shown in the figure.

claim: Articulating from the regenerated P2 in one mouse digit appears to be the beginning of the next phalangeal bone.
source: Moreover, articulating from the regenerated P2 appears to be the beginning of the next phalangeal bone (arrow, Figure 6k).
evidence: This is an observation from the experiment shown in the figure.

claim: The regenerative response observed in these mouse digits represents the most dramatic extent of self-organized mammalian digit regeneration reported thus far.
source: To our knowledge, the regenerative response observed in these digits represents the most dramatic extent of self-organized mammalian digit regeneration reported thus far.
evidence: This is a claim about the novelty and significance of the findings.

claim: Distal phalange regeneration in adult mice has not been reported.
source: Distal phalange regeneration in adults has not been reported, while interphalangeal joint formation from a P2 amputation has been achieved only through sequential Bmp administration (Yu et al., 2019) and there has been no documentation of the regrowth of the sesamoid bone.
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of knowledge in the field.

claim: Interphalangeal joint formation from a P2 amputation in mice has been achieved only through sequential Bmp administration.
source: Distal phalange regeneration in adults has not been reported, while interphalangeal joint formation from a P2 amputation has been achieved only through sequential Bmp administration (Yu et al., 2019) and there has been no documentation of the regrowth of the sesamoid bone.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: There has been no documentation of the regrowth of the sesamoid bone in mice.
source: Distal phalange regeneration in adults has not been reported, while interphalangeal joint formation from a P2 amputation has been achieved only through sequential Bmp administration (Yu et al., 2019) and there has been no documentation of the regrowth of the sesamoid bone.
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of knowledge in the field.

claim: The conserved effect of nutrient supplementation across three species that span more than 500 million years of evolutionary divergence suggests energetic parameters as ancestral regulators of regeneration activation in animals.
source: The conserved effect of nutrient supplementation across three species that span more than 500 million years of evolutionary divergence suggests energetic parameters as ancestral regulators of regeneration activation in animals.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the conserved effects across species.

claim: In mice, hypoxia coaxes cardiomyocytes to re-enter cell cycle.
source: While we did not test the regenerative effect of hypoxia beyond Aurelia, it is notable that in mice hypoxia coaxes cardiomyocytes to re-enter cell cycle (Kimura et al., 2015) and activate HIF1α promotes healing of ear hole punch injury (Zhang et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Activating HIF1α promotes healing of ear hole punch injury in mice.
source: While we did not test the regenerative effect of hypoxia beyond Aurelia, it is notable that in mice hypoxia coaxes cardiomyocytes to re-enter cell cycle (Kimura et al., 2015) and activate HIF1α promotes healing of ear hole punch injury (Zhang et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: In Aurelia, the amputation bisected through the body, and more than appendage was in fact regenerated, for example, circular muscle in the body is regrown.
source: Notably in Aurelia, the amputation bisected through the body, and more than appendage was in fact regenerated, for example, circular muscle in the body is regrown (Figure 2e).
evidence: This is an observation from the experiment shown in the figure.

claim: Nutrient supplementation may have regenerative effect in body parts beyond appendage.
source: Thus, nutrient supplementation may have regenerative effect in body parts beyond appendage.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observation of body tissue regeneration in Aurelia.

claim: Across animal phylogeny, some physiological features show interesting correlation with regenerative ability.
source: However, across animal phylogeny, some physiological features show interesting correlation with regenerative ability (Hariharan et al., 2016; Vivien et al., 2016; Sousounis et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Regeneration especially in vertebrates tends to decrease with age, with juveniles and larvae more likely to regenerate than adults.
source: First, regeneration especially in vertebrates tends to decrease with age, with juveniles and larvae more likely to regenerate than adults.
evidence: This is a statement about a known correlation in the field.

claim: The mammalian heart rapidly loses the ability to regenerate after birth.
source: For instance, the mammalian heart rapidly loses the ability to regenerate after birth and anurans cease to regenerate limbs upon metamorphosis.
evidence: This is a statement about a known phenomenon.

claim: Anurans cease to regenerate limbs upon metamorphosis.
source: For instance, the mammalian heart rapidly loses the ability to regenerate after birth and anurans cease to regenerate limbs upon metamorphosis.
evidence: This is a statement about a known phenomenon.

claim: Animals that continue to grow throughout life tend to also regenerate.
source: Second, animals that continue to grow throughout life tend to also regenerate.
evidence: This is a statement about a known correlation.

claim: Most annelids continue adding body segments and regenerate well.
source: For instance, most annelids continue adding body segments and regenerate well, a striking exception of which is leeches that make exactly 32 segments and one of the few annelids that do not regenerate body segments (Rouse, 1998).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Leeches make exactly 32 segments and are one of the few annelids that do not regenerate body segments.
source: For instance, most annelids continue adding body segments and regenerate well, a striking exception of which is leeches that make exactly 32 segments and one of the few annelids that do not regenerate body segments (Rouse, 1998).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Indeterminate growth is thought of as the ancestral state.
source: Consistent with the notion of regeneration as ancestral, indeterminate growth is thought of as the ancestral state (Hariharan et al., 2016).
